## Three questions {#overview}

::: {style="margin-top:110px;font-size:52px;line-height:1.4"}
- What can **we** do with agentic science **now**?
- How do we **engineer** this way of working?
- What do we want our own **practice** to become?
:::

::: notes
The arc moves from shared capabilities to engineering practice and then the personal choice
of what scientific practice should become. Leave the tension about agency implicit.
The tutorial offers a window into practical experience so people can make their own choices.
Cail usually finds this work very fun and enjoyable; it involves a different framing of work.
:::

::: notes
Scratch space: first explain that the axis is how long a human expert takes on tasks an agent
can complete with 50% reliability. It is not the agent's runtime. Mythos is near the suite's
measurement ceiling. The axes stay fixed. The sidebar first asks about human expert time for
a Millennium Prize Problem; advance once to replace the question with both case studies.
Cail's question: how long would a human need for a 50% chance of solving Navier–Stokes in 2026?
There is no measured human baseline. This motivates asking whether the individual-task framing
still captures what coordinated systems accomplish, rather than treating the case studies as
new METR measurements. The upper-right agent wall-time axis explicitly distinguishes these
case durations from the human-expert-time metric on the left.
88 × 10,000 = 880,000 is a constant-concurrency illustration, not measured agent-hours or human
work. The $6.5M is output-only pricing arithmetic, not actual disclosed internal cost.
Cail's possible HF joke: “they committed at least one felony.” This is a rhetorical joke, not
an established legal finding. The substantive point is the chain from a restricted environment
through multiple exploits into major machine-learning dataset infrastructure.
:::

## Yesterday’s frontier becomes cheap {#costs}

<div style="margin-top:45px">
<div style="font-size:42px;margin-bottom:40px">Navier–Stokes: 130B output tokens ≈ <strong>$6.5M</strong> at retail</div>
<div style="font-size:30px;color:#7A6F5C">ARC-AGI-1 · semi-private evaluation</div>
<div style="display:grid;grid-template-columns:1fr 130px 1fr;align-items:center;margin-top:40px">
<div><div style="font-size:38px">o3-preview · December 2024</div><div style="font-size:110px;color:#BC4538">$4,560</div><div style="font-size:36px">per task · 87.5%</div></div>
<div style="font-size:70px">→</div>
<div><div style="font-size:38px">DeepSeek-V4-Flash · July 2026</div><div style="font-size:110px;color:#3F8278">$0.021</div><div style="font-size:36px">per task · 87.0%</div></div>
</div>

<div style="border-top:1px solid #C5B89E;margin-top:40px;padding-top:25px;font-size:38px"><span style="color:#BC4538">Takeaway</span><br>Frontier moonshots may stay expensive.<br>Today’s hard problems can become cheap.</div>
<details style="font-size:28px;color:#7A6F5C;margin-top:24px;max-height:170px;overflow:auto"><summary style="cursor:pointer">Sources &amp; accounting notes</summary>
<p><a href="https://arcprize.org/blog/oai-o3-pub-breakthrough">ARC Prize: o3 score &amp; retrospective cost</a> · <a href="https://arcprize.org/results/deepseek-v4-flash-0731">ARC Prize: DeepSeek score &amp; cost</a> · <a href="https://openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution/">OpenAI: Navier–Stokes token count</a> · <a href="https://x.com/deredleritt3r/status/2098527713002672152">Prompted by prinz</a></p>
<p>ARC-AGI-1 semi-private evaluation; different systems and inference budgets. o3’s $4,560 is a retrospective estimate using o3-pro pricing. DeepSeek High: 87.0% at $0.021402901/task.</p>
<p><a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-6-astra">Astra retail output price: $50/M</a>. Navier–Stokes: 130B output tokens × $50/M = $6.5M, output-only retail equivalent, not disclosed internal spend. The benchmark comparison does not predict future Navier–Stokes cost.</p>
</details>
</div>

::: notes
The comparison is near-equal performance on the same ARC-AGI-1 semi-private benchmark category,
with different models and inference budgets. ARC retrospectively estimated the o3 high-compute
cost using o3-pro pricing in December 2025; this is not an actual December 2024 bill.
DeepSeek's High configuration scored 87.0% at $0.021402901/task. The cost ratio is about 213,000.
This motivates distinguishing the cost of demonstrating a capability from its later deployment
cost. It does not establish when an open model could solve Navier–Stokes, in how much time, or
at what cost. The tweet's 2028 prediction remains its author's speculation.
Navier pricing is a separate illustration, not a forecast or disclosed internal spend.
:::

:::

::: notes
~2 min, setting the stage with history. Two years ago — late 2024 — the way most of us touched
these models was this: a chatbot in a browser tab. The model was already smart, and the smart thing
to do was to treat it as an oracle: ask it for the code, then carry the intelligence out through the
clipboard, into your editor, where you fixed the imports, ran it, read the traceback, and went back
to ask again. Every loop through the problem passed through your hands. The model thought; you did
everything else. Hold onto that division of labor — the whole history I want to tell you is the
story of that division dissolving.
:::


## A harness closes the execution loop {#harness}

```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 1600 650" style="width:100%;max-height:730px;margin-top:45px" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="EB Garamond, Georgia, serif"><defs><marker id="middle-arrow-3" markerWidth="10" markerHeight="10" refX="8" refY="4" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L8 4 L0 8" fill="none" stroke="#7A6F5C" stroke-width="1.5"/></marker></defs><text x="800" y="45" text-anchor="middle" font-size="42" fill="#1B1611">“Write me a likelihood”</text><rect x="120" y="220" width="320" height="120" rx="12" fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="#BC4538" stroke-width="3"/><text x="280.0" y="293.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="38" fill="#BC4538">Model</text><path d="M440,280 L620,280" fill="none" stroke="#BC4538" stroke-width="4" marker-end="url(#middle-arrow-3)"/><rect x="620" y="220" width="360" height="120" rx="12" fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="#3D5BA0" stroke-width="3"/><text x="800.0" y="293.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="38" fill="#3D5BA0">Write likelihood.py</text><g class="fragment" data-fragment-index="0"><path d="M980,280 L1150,280" fill="none" stroke="#BC4538" stroke-width="4" marker-end="url(#middle-arrow-3)"/><rect x="1150" y="220" width="360" height="120" rx="12" fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="#3F8278" stroke-width="3"/><text x="1330.0" y="293.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="38" fill="#3F8278">Run via shell</text><text x="1330" y="400" text-anchor="middle" font-size="30" fill="#3F8278">python check_likelihood.py</text></g><g class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><path d="M1330 430 L1330 530 L280 530 L280 340" fill="none" stroke="#3F8278" stroke-width="4" marker-end="url(#middle-arrow-3)"/><text x="800" y="510" text-anchor="middle" font-size="38" fill="#3F8278">Output · errors · diagnostics</text></g><text x="800" y="625" text-anchor="middle" font-size="32" fill="#7A6F5C">Tool request → harness execution → model observation</text></svg>
```

<details style="font-size:26px;color:#7A6F5C;margin-top:10px"><summary>Sources &amp; notes</summary><a href="https://earendil.com/posts/what-is-a-harness/">Pi / Earendil · What is a Harness?</a> · <a href="https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-3-7-sonnet">Claude Code · February 2025</a> · <a href="https://claude.com/blog/building-agents-with-the-claude-agent-sdk">Tool-loop mechanics</a></details>

::: notes
Build on advance: writing code; then issuing a tool request that the harness executes; then returning output to the model for another step. The model emits a structured request, not an executable act by itself. Shell is one tool alongside file reads, edits, and search. Permissions and tool availability constrain execution. Claude Code made this pattern accessible in a terminal; tool use predates Claude Code. Introduce the loop before orchestration or subagents.
:::

::: notes
Context management concerns what is available to the next inference. Input and output share a finite budget, with model-specific limits. Tool access to a file does not put that file in context until it is read. Selection and summaries are lossy; preserve important decisions and evidence outside the conversation.
:::

## Cache the unchanged part of working memory {#prompt-caching}

```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 1600 650" style="width:100%;max-height:730px;margin-top:45px" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="EB Garamond, Georgia, serif"><defs><marker id="middle-arrow-4" markerWidth="10" markerHeight="10" refX="8" refY="4" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L8 4 L0 8" fill="none" stroke="#7A6F5C" stroke-width="1.5"/></marker></defs><text x="95" y="140" text-anchor="middle" fill="#3D5BA0">Reusable prefix</text><rect x="705" y="90" width="210" height="75" fill="#BC4538" fill-opacity=".15" stroke="#BC4538"/><text x="810" y="140" text-anchor="middle" font-size="32" fill="#BC4538">New context</text><text x="95" y="265" text-anchor="middle" font-size="32" fill="#7A6F5C">Step 2</text><rect x="190" y="215" width="710" height="75" fill="#3D5BA0" fill-opacity=".18" stroke="#3D5BA0"/><text x="545.0" y="265" text-anchor="middle" font-size="34" fill="#3D5BA0">Reusable prefix</text><rect x="915" y="215" width="210" height="75" fill="#BC4538" fill-opacity=".15" stroke="#BC4538"/><text x="1020" y="265" text-anchor="middle" font-size="32" fill="#BC4538">New context</text><text x="95" y="390" text-anchor="middle" font-size="32" fill="#7A6F5C">Step 3</text><rect x="190" y="340" width="920" height="75" fill="#3D5BA0" fill-opacity=".18" stroke="#3D5BA0"/><text x="650.0" y="390" text-anchor="middle" font-size="34" fill="#3D5BA0">Reusable prefix</text><rect x="1125" y="340" width="210" height="75" fill="#BC4538" fill-opacity=".15" stroke="#BC4538"/><text x="1230" y="390" text-anchor="middle" font-size="32" fill="#BC4538">New context</text><text x="800" y="535" text-anchor="middle" font-size="40" fill="#1B1611">Same prefix · reused computation · new suffix</text><text x="800" y="610" text-anchor="middle" font-size="34" fill="#7A6F5C">Input processing saved · context capacity unchanged</text></svg>
```

<details style="font-size:26px;color:#7A6F5C;margin-top:10px"><summary>Sources &amp; notes</summary><a href="https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching">Prompt caching mechanics</a></details>

::: notes
Build directly on the previous context-as-working-memory slide. The working set is still supplied to the model; caching reuses internal computation for an eligible unchanged prefix. This is not external memory, a smaller context, or a cache of finished answers. Schematic of repeated model requests. Cache hits require matching eligible prefixes and depend on provider retention and minimum lengths. They can reduce input cost and latency; they do not remove context limits or make generated output free. No universal cost multiplier or claim of zero prefill latency. Compaction trades prefix reuse against relevance and capacity; never-edit-history is not an absolute rule.
:::


::: notes
Analogy: context is working memory, files are persistent storage. An index helps find the relevant notes without loading everything. This is deliberate external memory management, not a guarantee of automatic recall. Save decisions with their assumptions and links to evidence. Results should be traceable to their inputs and configuration.
:::

## Skills make procedures reusable {#skills}

```{=html}
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1600 650" style="width:100%;height:auto" role="img" aria-label="An annotated skill document containing a trigger, scientific conventions, validation checks, and supporting scripts" font-family="EB Garamond, Georgia, serif"><text x="90" y="85" font-size="44" fill="#3F8278" text-anchor="start">Procedure, on demand</text><path d="M210 150 H760 L825 215 V560 H210 Z" fill="none" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="3" /><path d="M760 150 V215 H825" fill="none" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="3" /><text x="255" y="215" font-size="36" fill="#7A6F5C" text-anchor="start">SKILL.md</text><text x="255" y="295" font-size="48" fill="#3F8278" text-anchor="start">Fit a likelihood</text><path d="M255 342 H665" fill="none" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="5" /><path d="M255 364 H595" fill="none" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="5" /><path d="M255 452 H690" fill="none" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="5" /><path d="M255 474 H615" fill="none" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="5" /><path d="M255 496 H655" fill="none" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="5" /><rect x="250" y="390" width="525" height="35" fill="#3F8278" opacity="0.12"/><path d="M850 215 H955" fill="none" stroke="#7A6F5C" stroke-width="2" /><text x="990" y="227" font-size="40" fill="#7A6F5C" text-anchor="start">When to use it</text><path d="M850 315 H955" fill="none" stroke="#3F8278" stroke-width="2" /><text x="990" y="327" font-size="40" fill="#3F8278" text-anchor="start">Scientific conventions</text><path d="M850 410 H955" fill="none" stroke="#3F8278" stroke-width="2" /><text x="990" y="422" font-size="40" fill="#3F8278" text-anchor="start">Known-case checks</text><path d="M850 510 H955" fill="none" stroke="#3D5BA0" stroke-width="2" /><text x="990" y="522" font-size="40" fill="#3D5BA0" text-anchor="start">Scripts + references</text><text x="255" y="610" font-size="38" fill="#7A6F5C" text-anchor="start">Versioned · inspectable · reusable</text></svg>
```

::: notes
Skills package procedural guidance, often with references and helper scripts. They are instructions supplied to the model, not a guarantee that each step will execute. The selected scientific example is illustrative. Put checks in executable tools or hooks where reliable execution matters.
:::

## Hooks make checks event-driven {#hooks}

```{=html}
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1600 650" style="width:100%;height:auto" role="img" aria-label="A file edit interrupts the normal timeline with configured checks; failure returns actionable diagnostics for repair" font-family="EB Garamond, Georgia, serif"><text x="80" y="90" font-size="42" fill="#7A6F5C" text-anchor="start">Inside the harness</text><path d="M90 290 H1510" fill="none" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="5" /><circle cx="150" cy="290" r="12" fill="#3D5BA0" /><text x="150" y="355" font-size="40" fill="#3D5BA0" text-anchor="middle">Read</text><circle cx="490" cy="290" r="12" fill="#3D5BA0" /><text x="490" y="355" font-size="40" fill="#3D5BA0" text-anchor="middle">Edit</text><circle cx="1390" cy="290" r="12" fill="#3D5BA0" /><text x="1390" y="355" font-size="40" fill="#3D5BA0" text-anchor="middle">Continue</text><path d="M620 290 V155 H1120 V290" fill="none" stroke="#3F8278" stroke-width="5" /><text x="870" y="115" font-size="44" fill="#3F8278" text-anchor="middle">Configured hook</text><circle cx="680" cy="155" r="10" fill="#3F8278" /><circle cx="1050" cy="155" r="10" fill="#3F8278" /><text x="865" y="218" font-size="38" fill="#3F8278" text-anchor="middle">Units · known cases</text><path d="M1120 290 V485 H490 V390" fill="none" stroke="#BC4538" stroke-width="4" /><path d="M477 410 L490 390 L503 410" fill="none" stroke="#BC4538" stroke-width="3" /><text x="830" y="535" font-size="38" fill="#BC4538" text-anchor="middle">Failure → diagnostic → repair</text><text x="1480" y="610" font-size="36" fill="#7A6F5C" text-anchor="end">Event-triggered execution</text></svg>
```

::: notes
A configured hook runs on a defined harness event. Unlike a skill asking the model to remember a check, the trigger lives in the surrounding software. Whether a hook can block a tool or completion depends on the harness and event. Example is deliberately generic; a check still needs a scientifically meaningful assertion.
:::

## Delegate a piece of work without losing the thread {#delegation}

```{=html}
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1600 650" style="width:100%;margin-top:40px" font-family="EB Garamond,Georgia,serif"><path d="M220 300 H550 M710 300 H980" fill="none" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray=""/><circle cx="140" cy="300" r="80" fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="#BC4538" stroke-width="3"/><text x="140" y="312" text-anchor="middle" font-size="36" fill="#BC4538">You</text><circle cx="630" cy="300" r="80" fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="#3F8278" stroke-width="3"/><text x="630" y="312" text-anchor="middle" font-size="36" fill="#3F8278">Agent</text><text x="1090" y="245" text-anchor="middle" font-size="40" fill="#1B1611">Read · write · run</text><text x="1090" y="325" text-anchor="middle" font-size="34" fill="#1B1611">Code · tools · results</text><g class="fragment"><path d="M630 385 Q630 520 910 520" fill="none" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray=""/><circle cx="1000" cy="520" r="80" fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="#3D5BA0" stroke-width="3"/><text x="1000" y="532" text-anchor="middle" font-size="36" fill="#3D5BA0">Worker</text><text x="1280" y="450" text-anchor="middle" font-size="36" fill="#1B1611">A bounded question</text><text x="1280" y="525" text-anchor="middle" font-size="32" fill="#1B1611">Literature · code search</text><text x="1280" y="570" text-anchor="middle" font-size="32" fill="#1B1611">Implementation · review</text></g></svg>
```

::: notes
Start with user → main agent → tools. Advance adds a bounded worker with its own context. Examples include literature search, code investigation, review, and implementation. The main session carries the relationship with the user and integrates the result. Delegation is not necessarily parallel, and a returned summary is not proof of correctness.
:::

text-anchor="middle" font-size="31" fill="#3F8278">Frontier judgment</text><text x="620" y="480" text-anchor="middle" font-size="31" fill="#7A6F5C">Design · decomposition</text><text x="1370" y="535" text-anchor="middle" font-size="31" fill="#3D5BA0">Scoped tasks</text><text x="1370" y="576" text-anchor="middle" font-size="31" fill="#7A6F5C">Lower-cost models</text></svg>

::: notes
Message motion illustrates ongoing communication, not real telemetry. The lead can clarify scope, interrupt, redirect, and integrate emerging results; some systems also support peer messaging. This differs from fire-and-forget delegation. Shared goals, ownership, and communication discipline are necessary: more messages do not automatically mean better coordination. Preserve the user’s ability to steer. A strong, expensive lead can concentrate judgment in design and decomposition, giving lower-cost workers sufficiently clear task parameters. Model choice should follow task difficulty: review and ambiguous research can still need frontier intelligence. This is a useful allocation pattern, not a guarantee of lower total cost.
:::

fill="#3F8278">Code search</text><rect x="1050" y="110" width="320" height="80" fill="#BC4538" fill-opacity=".15" stroke="#BC4538"/><text x="1210" y="160" text-anchor="middle" font-size="34" fill="#BC4538">Review</text><rect x="350" y="480" width="390" height="70" fill="#BC4538" fill-opacity=".15" stroke="#BC4538"/><text x="530" y="525" text-anchor="middle" font-size="34" fill="#BC4538">Review</text><path d="M350 605 H1460" fill="none" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray=""/><text x="1360" y="645" text-anchor="middle" font-size="32" fill="#1B1611">Time →</text><path d="M970 280 V565" fill="none" stroke="#7A6F5C" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="6 8"/><text x="1180" y="430" text-anchor="middle" font-size="40" fill="#1B1611">Integrate the results</text><text x="1180" y="490" text-anchor="middle" font-size="32" fill="#7A6F5C">Dependencies · contention · cost</text></svg>

::: notes
Parallelization overlaps independent work. Schematic durations, not measured speedups. Join only when needed; the slowest required branch and integration cost limit the benefit. Avoid simultaneous conflicting writes; divide ownership or isolate workspaces. Extra workers spend extra resources. Independence and a plan for integrating evidence matter more than worker count.
:::

fill="#1B1611">Explicit dependencies · executable rules · inspectable control</text></svg>

::: notes
A task-specific program can define scatter/gather, adversarial review, checks, conditional retry, and acceptance. The forward dependency graph is DAG-like; the retry edge makes the overall program a loop, not literally a DAG. The orchestration is explicit code, while individual model calls remain stochastic. A failure can trigger bounded revision or human escalation. Link to the October 2025 Agent Builder image: graphs remain useful; code generation makes it practical to construct one for this task. People can inspect, modify, and approve its rules. This is one route toward coordinated swarms, not an inevitable evolution or a promise that model-generated orchestration is correct.
:::

::: notes
The slop cannon is a joke about unorganized throughput, not a claim that every generated artifact is worthless. Growing work can mix incompatible inputs, configurations, and outputs. Naming files is useful but insufficient: record which inputs, decisions, recipes, and outputs belong to each analysis. This motivates ASTRA without claiming a schema eliminates every provenance error. Distinguish remembering why a decision was made from validating that the current run used it.
:::

The official projects page describes lightcone-cli as the execution layer, with skills, agents, hooks, workflow support and execution manifests. A schema helps keep agents on track by making dependencies, decisions and evidence inspectable; it is not a guarantee of scientific correctness. No personal-membership line on the slide.

## ASTRA records the analysis; the agent does the work {#astra-intro}

::: {style="display:flex;justify-content:center;align-items:center;gap:90px;margin-top:90px"}
::: {style="width:44%"}
```yaml
# astra.yaml — machine-readable record
inputs:      # what goes in
outputs:     # what comes out
recipes:     # how, exactly
decisions:   # the choices that matter
evidence:    # verified against sources
```
:::
::: {style="width:40%"}
```bash
uv tool install astra-tools

claude plugin install \
  astra@lightcone-research
```
:::
:::

<details style="font-size:26px;color:#7A6F5C;margin-top:10px"><summary>Sources &amp; notes</summary><a href="https://astra-spec.org/">ASTRA specification</a></details>

::: notes
Two pieces of infrastructure, both installable in one line. ASTRA is a format — a YAML file that
is a machine-readable record of an analysis: its inputs, its outputs, the recipes that connect
them, and — the part I'll spend the most time on — the consequential methodological decisions, with
evidence that gets verified against the literature. ASTRA runs nothing; it validates and inspects.
The runner is the agent — the harness you just met. And the plugin teaches your agent the format:
the judgment about what counts as a decision, how to parameterize choices, when to split an
analysis. You install these two things, start your agent in an empty directory, and everything from
here on is prompts.
:::

## Measure dark energy in fifteen minutes {.section-divider #tutorial-open}

<div style="text-align:center;margin-top:90px;font-size:48px">580 supernovae · one parameter · an inspectable analysis</div>
<div style="text-align:center;margin-top:75px;font-size:32px"><a href="https://lightconeresearch.github.io/agent-skills/latest/astra/">ASTRA tutorial</a></div>

::: notes
A deliberately simple problem lets the audience watch execution, provenance, verification,
and methodological choices. Fifteen-minute live tutorial budget; the full exercise can take longer.
:::

## 1 · Kick off an analysis with Lightcone {#step-spec}

::: {.live-pair}
::: {.live-left}
::: {.prompt-card}
I'd like to use Lightcone tools to analyze the Union2.1 supernova compilation from the Supernova Cosmology Project. Let's write an ASTRA analysis that fits a flat LCDM model to this data and recovers Omega_Lambda.

Please produce two outputs: the best fit Omega_Lambda with uncertainties, and a downstream Hubble diagram figure with an absolute panel and a residuals panel. As you go, briefly walk me through each ASTRA element that you add; this is a live tutorial! Don't add any decisions yet.

<a class="prompt-source" data-copy-url href="https://supernova.lbl.gov/Union/figures/SCPUnion2.1_mu_vs_z.txt">Union2.1 data · SCPUnion2.1_mu_vs_z.txt ↗</a>
:::
:::
::: {.live-right}
::: {.watch-head}
while it runs — an illustrative spec
:::
```yaml
inputs:
  - id: union21
    type: data
    source: data/union21.txt

outputs:
  - id: best_fit
    type: metric
    inputs: [union21]
    recipe:
      command: python fit.py …
  - id: hubble_diagram
    type: figure
    inputs: [union21, best_fit]
    recipe:
      command: python plot.py …
```
:::
:::

::: notes
Step one: say what the analysis is, in words, and the agent writes the spec. Inputs: the data file.
Outputs: a best-fit — Omega Lambda with uncertainty, chi-squared — and a Hubble-diagram figure
downstream of it. Each output carries a recipe: the exact command that produces it, with the
dependencies explicit. Notice what this is: it's a DAG again! — but look who drew it. You said four
sentences of intent; the model wrote the graph, and a hook validated the file the moment it was
saved. The graph didn't disappear from science — provenance still wants a graph — it moved from
being the thing you hand-wire to being an artifact the agent maintains.
:::


## 2 · Did we reproduce the published result? {#step-verify}

::: {.live-pair}
::: {.live-left}
::: {.prompt-card}
The paper that published this catalogue is Suzuki et al. 2012, arXiv 1105.3470. Can we compare our Omega_Lambda to their supernova-only constraint?
:::
:::
::: {.live-right}
::: {.watch-head}
while it runs — what a verified claim looks like
:::
```yaml
prior_insights:
  suzuki_2012_result:
    claim: >
      [constraint from the paper]
      [assumptions + errors]
    evidence:
      - doi: >-
          10.48550/arXiv.1105.3470
        quote:
          exact: >
            [exact quote]
        location:
          value: "page=17"
```


:::
:::

::: notes
Step four: check it against the paper that published this catalogue — Suzuki et al. 2012. And
here's my favorite mechanism in the whole system. The agent caches the paper and records the
published constraint as a *prior insight* — a claim with evidence. The evidence is an exact quote,
with a page number — and ASTRA searches the cached PDF and verifies that the quote actually appears
on page seventeen. This matters because agents, like graduate students, occasionally remember
papers saying things they don't say. Claims about the literature are grounded in the literature,
mechanically. And with the quote verified, we can compare: they got 0.705, plus 0.040 minus 0.043.
Our central value agrees nicely. But look at the error bars — ours are three times tighter, on the
same 580 supernovae. Same data, same model. Something is wrong, and it's wrong in the direction
that should scare you: we're *too* confident.
:::


## 3 · What changes when we include systematics? {#step-decision}

::: {.live-pair}
::: {.live-left}
::: {.prompt-card}
Let's improve our systematics treatment to reproduce their published result. Track all changes as ASTRA decisions.
:::
:::
::: {.live-right}
::: {.watch-head}
add a decision · covariance treatment
:::
```yaml
decisions:
  covariance:
    label: Covariance treatment
    rationale: Account for systematics
    default: full
    options:
      stat_only:
        label: Statistical only
      full:
        label: Statistical + systematic

outputs:
  best_fit:
    decisions: [covariance]
    # recipe uses the selected option
```
:::
:::

::: notes
Step five, and the payoff. We ask the agent to find out why: download the two Union2.1 covariance
files — with and without systematics — work out which one our error column corresponds to, and
record a *decision* in the spec: statistical-only versus full systematic covariance. The answer:
our fit had been using the no-systematics errors — the error column in the data file *is* the diagonal
of the no-systematics covariance, to twelve decimal places. Everything the systematic covariance knows was
sitting in a file we had never opened. Switch to it, and watch the plot: the central value barely
moves — 0.722 to 0.714 — but the uncertainty more than doubles, and only then does our measurement
actually lie beside the published one: 0.2 sigma apart, their data, their systematics, their
method. Here's the lesson, and it's the sentence I'd have you take home: if you had ranked this
choice by its effect on the best-fit number, it would have looked nearly irrelevant. It is the
difference between a number that *resembles* theirs and a number you can *put beside* theirs. That
is what a decision is — and this field, all of science, is made of thousands of them, almost none
of them written down. ASTRA writes them down.
:::



## Give the agent a task, not just a question {#longhorizon-tasks}

<div style="display:grid;grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr;gap:100px;margin-top:110px">
<div style="border-top:4px solid #C5B89E;padding-top:35px"><div style="font-size:36px;color:#7A6F5C">An answer</div><div style="font-size:52px;margin-top:35px">How would I fit this?</div></div>
<div style="border-top:4px solid #3F8278;padding-top:35px"><div style="font-size:36px;color:#3F8278">A piece of work</div><div style="font-size:52px;margin-top:35px">Fit · check · report</div><div style="font-size:36px;margin-top:45px">Inputs · authority · acceptance criteria</div></div>
</div>

::: notes
Return to the hurdle introduced by the clipboard: chatting with Claude is not yet delegating
execution. Asking questions remains useful for learning and reflection; the limitation is having
to carry every action between the answer and the world. A task gives the system permission,
tools, and a way to tell whether the work is acceptable. Long-horizon work needs checkpoints,
budgets, and escalation rather than unlimited unattended action. No Shuttle demonstration needed.
:::

## Turn repeated work into a reusable practice {#reusable-practice}

```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 1600 650" style="width:100%;margin-top:60px" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="EB Garamond,Georgia,serif">
<g fill="none" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="3"><path d="M100 200 Q230 90 360 200 T620 200"/><path d="M100 320 Q230 210 360 320 T620 320"/><path d="M100 440 Q230 330 360 440 T620 440"/></g>
<g font-size="38" fill="#7A6F5C" text-anchor="middle"><text x="350" y="90">Repeated manual effort</text><text x="350" y="560">Same task · another session</text></g>
<path d="M750 100 L750 580" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="2"/>
<path d="M950 145 H1330 L1410 225 V540 H950 Z M1330 145 V225 H1410" fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="#3F8278" stroke-width="3"/>
<g font-size="40" fill="#3F8278"><text x="990" y="270">Procedure</text><text x="990" y="365">Executable checks</text><text x="990" y="460">Evidence + examples</text></g>
<text x="1180" y="90" font-size="38" fill="#1B1611" text-anchor="middle">Capture the generalizable part</text>
<text x="1180" y="610" font-size="34" fill="#7A6F5C" text-anchor="middle">Version · reuse · improve</text>
</svg>
```

::: notes
Cail's practical aspiration: when a task repeats, stop doing the same handwork and teach the
system the reusable procedure. A skill or script captures instructions; tests and reference
cases capture what success means. Not every first attempt deserves automation: stabilize the
scientific intent before generalizing. Reliability comes from the surrounding engineering,
not from pretending stochastic model output is deterministic. Keep human review for choices
that cannot be adequately checked automatically.
:::

## Search, inspect, follow the thread {#search-as-action}

```{=html}
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1600 650" style="width:100%;margin-top:50px" font-family="EB Garamond,Georgia,serif"><text x="90" y="80" font-size="48" fill="#1B1611">“Why did we change the covariance?”</text><path d="M120 150 V540 H1450" fill="none" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="180" cy="540" r="9" fill="#3F8278"/><text x="150" y="605" font-size="34" fill="#1B1611">Search</text><circle cx="650" cy="540" r="9" fill="#3F8278"/><text x="620" y="605" font-size="34" fill="#1B1611">Inspect</text><circle cx="1190" cy="540" r="9" fill="#3F8278"/><text x="1160" y="605" font-size="34" fill="#1B1611">Follow</text><text x="155" y="245" font-size="36" fill="#3F8278">grep · filenames · indexes</text><text x="155" y="305" font-size="34" fill="#1B1611">covariance / systematics</text><g class="fragment"><path d="M570 190 h300 l40 40 v160 h-340 Z m300 0 v40 h40" fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="2"/><text x="590" y="290" font-size="34" fill="#1B1611">Meeting notes</text><text x="585" y="425" font-size="34" fill="#3F8278">Decision → experiment 12</text></g><g class="fragment"><path d="M1080 190 h300 l40 40 v160 h-340 Z m300 0 v40 h40" fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="2"/><text x="1100" y="290" font-size="34" fill="#1B1611">Experiment 12</text><text x="1080" y="425" font-size="34" fill="#3F8278">Inputs · result · rationale</text><path d="M900 285 Q970 180 1080 285" fill="none" stroke="#3F8278" stroke-width="3"/></g></svg>
```

::: notes
An illustrative retrieval episode, not a claim about a specific meeting. An agent can search, read, refine the query, and follow links. grep is a useful primitive; semantic retrieval and vector stores can still help. The point is iterative retrieval under the model’s control, not that one search technology makes all others obsolete. No historical popularity claim is needed.
:::

## A wiki gives knowledge an address {#wiki-primitive}

```{=html}
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1600 650" style="width:100%;margin-top:50px" font-family="EB Garamond,Georgia,serif"><path d="M610 215 h300 l40 40 v160 h-340 Z m300 0 v40 h40" fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="2"/><text x="630" y="315" font-size="34" fill="#1B1611">Covariance choices</text><path d="M80 65 h300 l40 40 v160 h-340 Z m300 0 v40 h40" fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="2"/><text x="100" y="165" font-size="34" fill="#1B1611">Meeting notes</text><path d="M80 395 h300 l40 40 v160 h-340 Z m300 0 v40 h40" fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="2"/><text x="100" y="495" font-size="34" fill="#1B1611">Paper + quotation</text><path d="M1160 65 h300 l40 40 v160 h-340 Z m300 0 v40 h40" fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="2"/><text x="1180" y="165" font-size="34" fill="#1B1611">Experiment record</text><path d="M1160 395 h300 l40 40 v160 h-340 Z m300 0 v40 h40" fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="2"/><text x="1180" y="495" font-size="34" fill="#1B1611">Project index</text><g stroke="#3F8278" stroke-width="3" fill="none"><path d="M420 165 Q540 165 610 290"/><path d="M420 495 Q540 495 610 350"/><path d="M950 290 Q1050 165 1160 165"/><path d="M950 350 Q1050 495 1160 495"/></g><text x="620" y="180" font-size="36" fill="#3F8278">A named, linked page</text><text x="585" y="585" font-size="36" fill="#1B1611">Index · links · sources · upkeep</text></svg>
```

::: notes
A wiki is an organizing primitive in the toolbox, not a complete external brain or a guarantee of recall. Named pages and indexes make knowledge findable; links preserve relationships; sources let claims be checked. Markdown files can serve this purpose without a dedicated wiki application. Keep raw records and provenance accessible, and update or mark stale summaries. This builds on the earlier working-memory versus persistent-storage distinction.
:::

## Past work becomes material for new work {#knowledge-compounds}

```{=html}
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1600 650" style="width:100%;margin-top:50px" font-family="EB Garamond,Georgia,serif"><text x="80" y="75" font-size="42" fill="#7A6F5C">Accumulated work</text><path d="M80 130 h300 l40 40 v160 h-340 Z m300 0 v40 h40" fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="2"/><text x="100" y="230" font-size="34" fill="#1B1611">Project A · a method</text><path d="M80 390 h300 l40 40 v160 h-340 Z m300 0 v40 h40" fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="2"/><text x="100" y="490" font-size="34" fill="#1B1611">Project B · a caveat</text><path d="M440 225 Q740 225 880 335 M440 485 Q740 485 880 335" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="3" fill="none"/><circle cx="900" cy="335" r="13" fill="#BC4538"/><text x="670" y="120" font-size="44" fill="#1B1611">A new question</text><g class="fragment"><path d="M920 335 H1120" stroke="#3F8278" stroke-width="4"/><path d="M1120 235 h300 l40 40 v160 h-340 Z m300 0 v40 h40" fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="2"/><text x="1140" y="335" font-size="34" fill="#1B1611">Candidate connection</text><text x="1120" y="520" font-size="34" fill="#3F8278">Trace back · test · retain</text></g><text x="545" y="605" font-size="42" fill="#1B1611">Searchable records × new questions</text></svg>
```

::: notes
The compounding value is reusable knowledge: previous work can inform a question in another project. Cail describes using LLMs as a filesystem: remembering meaning approximately and asking the agent to recover the source. Cross-project synthesis is a possibility to investigate, not evidence that a proposed connection is correct. Keep the distinction between discovering a candidate and validating its applicability. No unverified mathematical breakthrough example is asserted.
:::

::: notes
A loop is a way to spend more effort, not a guarantee of improvement. Define the goal, observable evaluation, stopping rule, and when to return to the human. Example: parameter recovery on synthetic data with a stated tolerance. Independent checks matter because repeating the same blind spot can reinforce it.
:::

effort</text><text x="1450" y="75" font-size="42" fill="#BC4538" text-anchor="end">Scientific judgment</text><path d="M100 190 C280 155 350 215 580 190" fill="none" stroke="#3D5BA0" stroke-width="3" /><circle cx="105" cy="190" r="6" fill="#3D5BA0" /><path d="M100 260 C280 225 350 285 580 260" fill="none" stroke="#3D5BA0" stroke-width="3" /><circle cx="105" cy="260" r="6" fill="#3D5BA0" /><path stroke="#3D5BA0" stroke-width="3" /><circle cx="105" cy="400" r="6" fill="#3D5BA0" /><path d="M100 470 C280 435 350 495 580 470" fill="none" stroke="#3D5BA0" stroke-width="3" /><circle cx="105" cy="470" r="6" fill="#3D5BA0" /><path d="M600 135 V505" fill="none" stroke="#3F8278" stroke-width="7" /><text x="600" y="565" font-size="38" fill="#3F8278" text-anchor="middle">Units</text><path stroke="#3F8278" stroke-width="7" /><text x="1100" y="565" font-size="38" fill="#3F8278" text-anchor="middle">Recovery</text><path d="M600 190 H1420 M600 400 H1420" fill="none" stroke="#3F8278" stroke-width="4" /><circle cx="1440" cy="190" r="14" fill="#3F8278" /><circle cx="1440" cy="400" r="14" fill="#3F8278" /><path d="M600 260 H850 M600 470 H850" fill="none" stroke="#3D5BA0" stroke-width="3" /><path d="M588 318 L612 342 M588 342 L612 318" fill="none" stroke="#BC4538" stroke-width="4" /><path d="M838 248 L862 272 M838 272 L862 248" fill="none" stroke="#BC4538" stroke-width="4" /><path d="M838 458 L862 482 M838 482 L862 458" fill="none" stroke="#BC4538" stroke-width="4" /><path d="M850 470 C850 635 250 640 130 530" fill="none" stroke="#BC4538" stroke-width="3" /><text x="320" y="610" font-size="38" fill="#BC4538" text-anchor="start">Repair</text><text x="1440" y="315" font-size="40" fill="#3F8278" text-anchor="middle">Review</text><text x="1000" y="625" font-size="38" fill="#7A6F5C" text-anchor="start">Checks encode decisions</text></svg>

::: notes
Backpressure means actionable resistance to invalid progress: failed validation, withheld acceptance, or escalation. Engineering checks carries human decisions into repeated work, letting attention move to higher-level choices. Passing a test suite is not proof of scientific truth. Include model misspecification, held-out cases, provenance, and independent scientific review; do not optimize solely against an easy proxy.
:::

## Do you still need to read code? {#read-code}

<div style="display:grid;grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr;gap:70px;align-items:center;margin-top:65px">
<div style="font-size:42px;line-height:1.5"><div style="color:#3F8278;margin-bottom:40px">Understand the implementation</div><div>Ask for a walkthrough</div><div style="font-size:32px;color:#7A6F5C">Assumptions · data flow · examples</div><div style="margin-top:35px">Read the critical core</div><div style="font-size:32px;color:#7A6F5C">Likelihood · units · interfaces</div></div>
<svg viewBox="0 0 720 530" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%"><rect x="20" y="20" width="680" height="480" rx="14" fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="2"/><text x="55" y="75" fill="#7A6F5C" font-size="28" font-family="monospace">likelihood.py</text><g stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="9" stroke-linecap="round"><path d="M60 120 H310 M85 160 H490 M85 200 H380 M85 365 H460 M60 410 H295 M85 450 H370"/></g><rect x="40" y="233" width="640" height="98" fill="#E0EAE3" rx="5"/><text x="65" y="272" fill="#3F8278" font-size="26" font-family="monospace">r = data - model</text><text x="65" y="310" fill="#3F8278" font-size="26" font-family="monospace">chi2 = r.T @ solve(cov, r)</text></svg>
</div>

::: notes
Understanding is the obligation; line-by-line reading is one means. An agent walkthrough can
be an effective entry point, but an explanation can be wrong too. Check explanations against
actual source and behavior. Direct inspection is especially worthwhile where a small mistake
propagates through the analysis: scientific assumptions, core interfaces, and shared primitives.
:::

<div style="display:grid;grid-template-columns:38% 58%;gap:4%;align-items:center;margin-top:45px">
<div style="font-size:38px;line-height:1.7">HTML report<br><span style="color:#7A6F5C">Plots · comparisons<br>Checks · caveats<br>Links to artifacts</span></div>
<div style="border:2px solid #C5B89E;border-radius:12px;background:#FBF6E9;padding:32px;box-shadow:0 8px 24px #1b161110">
<div style="font-size:34px;border-bottom:1px solid #C5B89E;padding-bottom:18px">Analysis review <span style="float:right;font-size:23px;color:#7A6F5C">schematic</span></div>
<svg viewBox="0 0 750 280" style="width:100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M55 25 V230 H715" stroke="#C5B89E" fill="none" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M60 210 Q190 80 330 100 T710 40" fill="none" stroke="#3F8278" stroke-width="5"/><path d="M60 195 Q190 110 330 120 T710 65" fill="none" stroke="#BC4538" stroke-width="4" stroke-dasharray="10 8"/><text x="430" y="255" font-size="24" font-family="Georgia" fill="#7A6F5C">baseline / revised analysis</text></svg>
<div style="display:flex;justify-content:space-between;font-size:28px;color:#7A6F5C;border-top:1px solid #C5B89E;padding-top:20px">Evidence <span>Open questions</span><span>Inspect files ↗</span></div>
</div>
</div>

::: notes
Programmatic checks do not replace looking at the results. Ask the agent to prepare a concise
HTML report with real plots, comparisons, validation results, caveats, and links to the exact
artifacts and code. Review those results yourself. A polished report is a review surface, not
proof of correctness. The figure on this slide is explicitly schematic, not a scientific result.
:::

Long-running work makes concurrent tasks natural. Track objective, status, blockers, checkpoints,
and the evidence needed for acceptance independently of individual chat windows. Symphony is
an example of board-driven orchestration, not a required tool. Keep the personal tooling aside
oral; no custom-system demonstration is needed here.
:::

## The meta-skill: knowing what is computationally tractable {#ball-2}

::: {style="display:flex;justify-content:center;margin-top:110px"}
::: {.quote-card style="max-width:1400px"}
"if you can master the meta-skill of figuring out what problems in arbitrary domains are
computationally tractable … you'll have refined heuristics for the right questions to ask about
everything. … **this is probably the skill to have optimized for** … though I readily admit I don't
know how long it will remain a human advantage. **it is for now though.**"

::: {.quote-attrib}
Dean W. Ball — August 8, 2026
:::
:::
:::

::: notes
Second claim, and this one is about you. The scarce skill in this regime is not coding and it's
not prompting — it's the meta-skill of looking at an arbitrary domain and knowing which of its
problems are computationally tractable, and what question to ask to make progress along the
margin. Master that and you get to be, in his phrase, a kind of meta-genius — for at least a year
or two, maybe longer. Everyone in this room is unusually well positioned for this: physics-informed
ML is *already* the discipline of knowing what physics can be pushed through computation. But
notice the honesty of the last clause: he doesn't know how long it remains a human advantage. It is
for now. The meta-skill is temporary — and that's not a reason for despair, it's a reason for
urgency and, honestly, for joy: this is the window in which knowing how to do this makes you
extraordinary.
:::


## The stake in the ground {#stake}

::: {style="display:flex;justify-content:center;align-items:center;margin-top:160px"}
::: {style="max-width:1400px;text-align:center;font-size:1.35em;line-height:1.45"}
In five years, I expect frontier AI to be **better at astrophysics and cosmology than the vast
majority of currently employed astrophysicists and cosmologists** — to the extent that the
economics of our field are drastically changed.
:::
:::

::: notes
So let me put a stake in the ground — a concrete, falsifiable position you can hold me to. In five
years, I expect frontier AI to be better at astrophysics and cosmology than the vast majority of
currently employed astrophysicists and cosmologists — to the point that the economics of our field
are drastically changed. I might be wrong! It's a prediction, and predictions about exponentials
are hard in both directions. But notice that everything you saw today — the harness, the tutorial,
the verified analysis — is the current state, distinct from this forecast. If you think I'm wrong,
I'd genuinely love to argue about it in the discussion. If I'm right, then the interesting question
isn't whether — it's what you personally do about it.
:::

[**An economy of contribution**]{style="font-size:1.08em;color:#3F8278"}

::: {style="flex:1;display:flex;flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;color:#1B1611;padding-bottom:2.5em"}
[« …l'augmentation du savoir des travailleurs à travers un nouvel agencement entre la machine et le travailleur »]{style="display:block;text-align:center;font-size:0.98em;line-height:1.5;padding:0 0.2em"}

[— Bernard Stiegler]{style="display:block;text-align:right;color:#3F8278;font-size:0.9em;letter-spacing:0.02em;margin-top:0.55em"}
:::
:::

:::
::::::::::::::

::: notes
~1.5 min. [Lifted from CNRS `#the-choice` — the frame is a DRAFT for you to make your own; the
first-person passage at the end is yours, keep verbatim.] Before I put the choice to you personally,
the collective version — and I get to use a Greek word in Crete. *Pharmakon*: the remedy that is
also the poison, one dose, both faces at once. Which face science gets is not decided by the
technology; it's decided by the practice we build around it.

The poison — "AI science factories." Not hypothetical: papers already framed as *Competing with AI
Scientists*, the John Henry race humans are built to lose; a *Parallel ArXiv* where agents write the
papers and agents review them — a literature with no one in it. What's lost isn't jobs, it's the
*doing* of science. And a structural loss underneath: once people are out of the loop, output is a
function of capital — the labs have every incentive to stop selling the tools and do the science
in-house. Discovery scales with capital, not expertise.

The cure — same tools, different practice. The grunt work goes to the agents; the human is freed for
the science that matters — you talk to the model, it hands you a plot, you argue about it with a
colleague on a walk, and the argument becomes the next set of actions. Not agent fleets replacing
people, not the lone genius — networks of humans amplified by agents. Stiegler called it an
*économie de la contribution*: the machine augments the worker's knowledge rather than displacing it.

[Cail's, verbatim:] This is not only about jobs. It is about keeping the part of the work we
actually love — discovery. I would far rather spend this era in wonderful, beautiful discovery,
amplified, than watch the work get slowly ripped from our hands by agent "competitors." If a day
comes when there is nothing left for us to add, so be it — but I would rather enjoy the good times
while they last, and shape the practice so people stay *in* it.
:::

:::

::: notes
And here is the honest framing of that choice, because I want to be careful: neither path is bad —
it depends on what you want. One real option: find a niche where things don't scale — where data is
scarce, where the loop runs through hardware, through a wet lab, through people — and hold on a
while longer. Those eddies exist and they are legitimate places to do beautiful science. The other:
use exactly this window to become an expert in scaling — in the meta-skill — and move with the wave
to see what comes next. What I'd argue against is only the default: drifting into one of these by
not choosing. Think about the futures you'd actually want to live in — including the uncomfortable
ones — so that you can genuinely advocate for what you want in the world.
:::

## Stable principles are emerging for agentic science {#principles data-visibility="uncounted"}

Verification
:::

:::
:::

Looping
:::

towards a desired state<br>a constitution rather than a plan
:::

::: {.column style="width:27%;text-align:center;padding:0 1em;border-left:1px solid #d9cdb4"}

::::::::::::::

::: {style="text-align:center;margin-top:2.4em"}
```{=html}
<div class="r-stack" style="justify-items:center">
<pre class="fragment fade-out" data-fragment-index="1" style="display:inline-block;justify-self:center;text-align:left;background:#FBF6E9;border:1px solid #C5B89E;border-radius:14px;padding:0.8em 1.5em;font-family:'IBM Plex Mono',ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:0.72em;line-height:1.6;color:#3a342b;box-shadow:0 1px 5px rgba(0,0,0,0.05);width:fit-content;margin:0 auto"><span style="color:#7a6f5c"># an agent is an LLM in a loop</span>
<span style="color:#3F8278">context</span> = startup_context + user_prompt
<span style="color:#bc4538">while</span> <span style="color:#bc4538">not</span> done:
    response = llm(<span style="color:#3F8278">context</span>)
    <span style="color:#3F8278">context</span> += execute(response.tool_calls)</pre>
<pre class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1" style="display:inline-block;justify-self:center;text-align:left;background:#FBF6E9;border:1px solid #C5B89E;border-radius:14px;padding:0.8em 1.5em;font-family:'IBM Plex Mono',ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:0.72em;line-height:1.6;color:#3a342b;box-shadow:0 1px 5px rgba(0,0,0,0.05);width:fit-content;margin:0 auto"><span style="color:#7a6f5c"># the same loop, around whole sessions</span>
<span style="color:#3F8278">constitution</span> = user_intent
<span style="color:#bc4538">while</span> <span style="color:#bc4538">not</span> done:
    state = get_state(environment, <span style="color:#3F8278">constitution</span>)  <span style="color:#7a6f5c"># unbiased assessment of state</span>
    implement(state, <span style="color:#3F8278">constitution</span>)
    amend(<span style="color:#3F8278">constitution</span>)  <span style="color:#7a6f5c"># open-ended research</span></pre>
</div>
```
:::

::: notes
~2 min. [Lifted from the CNRS deck — Cail's rehearsed script, lightly retargeted.] The specific
techniques change every month as the models get better — what I did last July looks nothing like
what I do now. But underneath that churn, three principles have stayed stable. These are what I'd
teach.

**Verify.** The moment agents can do a lot, verification becomes the bottleneck — you can generate
far more than you can check. So you organize the work around making the checks cheap and
high-signal, and more fundamentally you design the work so the checks are built in. Tests are the
obvious case — but real science has no ground truth to test against; the data is real, the answer
is unknown, and a "check" can be a subtle, nuanced judgment. You saw a small version in the
tutorial: the verified quote, the recorded decision. At scale it becomes a design problem: name the
things that must be true if the work is right, and check them as you go.

**Loop toward a desired state.** The central object is the loop. An agent just is an LLM in a
loop — act, observe, update, repeat. The next level of abstraction is to put a loop around whole
sessions: each one starts from a fresh context. And what you hand each session matters: for
open-ended research, a rigid plan is often counterproductive — it forces you to foresee everything
and can't adapt to what the results tell you. Instead you write a constitution: it describes the
desired state; the current state is discoverable from the environment. A goal to reach, not a plan
to follow. Notice this is the same inversion as the harness slide — you stop drawing the graph at
the session level too.

**Accumulate context.** You quickly start doing more than you can possibly remember — what you've
already checked, what's true, what failed. You have to take notes, and you can't do it by hand. So
you need a memory system: as much context as possible in a form that's searchable, with progressive
disclosure — summaries that open into detail. This is what keeps the work honest: it's how you
avoid hallucinating, and how you know what ground you've already covered.

If you remember three things: verification, looping, accumulation.
:::

![](images/cosebis_bsigma_talk.png){.blend-figure width=92% fig-align="center"}

::: notes
~2 min. [Lifted from CNRS — Cail's rehearsed script, with a two-sentence setup added for a room that
hasn't seen the UNIONS science; DRAFT the setup in your own words.] Here's what verification looks
like on the real thing. Setup, in two sentences: gravitational lensing distorts galaxy shapes in a
pattern that has no curl — physics forbids the swirling "B-mode" — so any B-mode we measure has to be
contamination, and hunting it is the daily craft of the field. We measure it three independent ways
— correlation functions in configuration space, power spectra in harmonic space, and COSEBIs, the
sharp discrete modes both of those compress into — and with agents doing the labor, we could afford
to run all three, with full covariances, on every version of the catalogue.

Now the plot. Don't read the axes; read the shape. On the left, points that should sit on the flat
line instead climb away from it: a swirl that physics forbids, so it *must* be contamination. Two of
our three measures had passed; this third, sharper one caught it, because it concentrates a small
fingerprint the others dilute below notice. We could even pin down its size — it repeats at the
spacing of the camera's individual sensors, a man-made scale where the instrument would imprint
itself. Right panel: after we cut the affected range, it sits back on the line. The move to land:
the disagreement isn't a failure of the analysis, it's the analysis *working* — the measurement
telling us where the instrument was lying. And this is the honest version of "agents help": not
doing the same analysis faster, but doing a *more rigorous* one, because you can now check at a
finer level than any human team could afford.
:::

::: notes
~1.5 min. [Lifted from CNRS — Cail's rehearsed script, near-verbatim.] The agentic explosion,
measured honestly, plus the practice that drove it. I started doing this work with agents in July
2025 — the shaded era. The honest measure of work isn't net lines (they cancel) or commit counts
(gameable); it's everything I touched, written plus deleted. By that measure 2026 Q1 is
twenty-two thousand lines even though it nets to almost zero, because agentic work is relentless
iteration and refactoring. My output grew roughly six-fold and came to match my three closest
collaborators combined — one person doing the work of a small team. And the row below is the
practice I built as I went, on the same timeline: loops, then a memory system, then constitutions,
then the move from chat sessions to autonomous tasks, and finally Lightcone — the open ecosystem
where tools like ASTRA live. This chart is the talk's title made concrete: the labor scales.
:::

::: notes
~1.5 min. [Lifted from CNRS close — Cail's rehearsed script, retargeted from "the program" to "the
practice".] This is how it all composes, as a flywheel. I pour in what a cosmologist knows — but
collaboratively: meeting transcripts, the team's vetted wikis, shared judgment. That becomes the
objectives and the verification pressure that shape a funnel; inside it, long-horizon agent loops
do an enormous amount of labor without drifting. Out come live reports I can actually read and
check — and the best of what I learn flows back into the expertise that steers the next turn. A
small amount of human judgment, encoded and refined each cycle, steers a vast amount of machine
labor toward results I can stand behind. That's what made a small team's analysis tractable this
year — and it's the shape I think scientific collaborations drift toward generally. Which brings
us to what this means for all of us.
:::

## Astrophysics has become an information science {#ball-1 data-visibility="uncounted"}

::: {style="display:flex;justify-content:center;margin-top:110px"}
::: {.quote-card style="max-width:1400px"}
"…if every current prosumer-tier subscriber to codex and claude code donated a tiny share of their
monthly compute, **we will soon be able to automate more astrophysics than is currently done by
human astrophysicists** — the ones who operate in the 'astrophysics as data science' regime at
least."

::: {.quote-attrib}
Dean W. Ball — August 8, 2026
:::
:::
:::

::: notes
So what does it mean? Let me borrow two claims from Dean Ball — a policy researcher, not an AI
booster — writing three weeks ago. First claim: some sciences, astrophysics chief among them, have
in practice become information sciences — high-capex shared instruments producing data, plus labor
that is almost entirely computation on that data. And in that regime, the arithmetic is brutal: the
idle compute of the world's coding-agent subscribers is soon enough to automate more astrophysics
than human astrophysicists currently do. You just watched the existence proof: a dark-energy
measurement, spec'd, run, verified against the literature, by an agent, in minutes. He's talking
about us. This is coming right for our field, and I think both of his claims are true.
:::

::: notes
~1.5 min. [Lifted from CNRS `#sim-bench-rl` — retargeted from "my program" to "what this room can
do"; DRAFT, refine to your voice.] And here is where the meta-skill lands on *this* room
specifically. The first places AI got genuinely productive were the verifiable ones — code, math —
because you can check the answer and train on it at scale. Physics has no answer key: one universe,
no re-runs. But look at what you already build. Top row: full-physics simulations, fast surrogates,
simulation-based inference — a mature ecosystem whose whole purpose is to run the analysis on a
universe whose answer we *do* know. [advance] That is exactly the substrate agents are missing.
Your expertise and your simulations become benchmarks that characterise real scientific work;
instantiated in simulation, where the truth is known, they become RL environments — a reward to
train agents on. And it flows back: every environment is traceable to the people it came from, so
the value returns to its source rather than to whoever has the most compute. Two things to say out
loud for an ML audience. First, the reward is sparse and *noisy* — you can do everything right and
still land two sigma off by chance; learning efficiently from a reward that noisy is a real, open
AI problem, and physics is the place to crack it. Second, everything is hackable, this included —
the fix isn't an unhackable reward, it's closing the sim-to-real gap so the local hacking stays
honest. Physics-informed ML is not a consumer of this transition. It is the supply chain.
:::

::: notes
~1 min. [Lifted from CNRS; retargeted — DRAFT, refine to your voice.] Here's what the looping
principle looks like in my actual working day. Early on I worked the way everyone does — one prompt
at a time, steering each step myself. Now I mostly hand agents long-horizon tasks and let them run.
This is my real task board: each card is an agent working a piece of the analysis on its own — some
drafting, some in flight, some waiting on my review. And when one finishes — [advance] — it hands
back a full write-up of a real result: here a shear-catalog cross-check, figures and numbers ready
for me to check. My job moved up a level: from doing each step to designing the tasks and verifying
what comes back. The constitutions those agents run on are exactly the astra.yaml idea grown up:
specs that describe the desired state of a piece of science.
:::

::: notes
Backup, for the verification discussion. [CNRS `#blinding`, Cail's script.] The discipline that
replaces a ground truth. Left: there's a truth, and the rest of the field clustered near it — and a
real pull to land your own result next to everyone else's. That pull is confirmation bias. Right: so
we blind ourselves — shift our number by a secret amount and hide where the field sits, so while we
make every analysis choice we genuinely can't tell how far we are from anyone. Only once every choice
is frozen do we unblind. For this room: it is exactly holding out a test set — you cannot tune toward
a number you cannot see. And note it composes with agents perfectly: the agent can make and record
every decision, and still never see the answer.
:::
